431.quote_or_event: “He will sink through anger; he will go down through pride; delusion will block up his path; through greed he will incur dangers in both worlds.”
431.explanation: King Nami, renouncing his throne, names the passions (kashāyas) that ruin a person: anger, pride, delusion and greed. Indra then praises him for having conquered each of them.
431.tie_back: Valluvar says only those free of arrogance, anger and base desire turn prosperity into true dignity; Nami, a king himself, names the same cluster of faults as the cause of a person's fall.
431._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit: pride, anger and craving appear in both lists. The Jain verse adds delusion, and its aim is liberation rather than a ruler's honoured prosperity.

432.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
432.explanation: This verse from the Saman Suttam anthology sets out what each of the four passions destroys, and singles out greed as the one that ruins everything.
432.tie_back: Valluvar names avarice and false pride among the faults that harm a ruler; the Jain verse likewise picks out greed and pride as destroyers, with greed the most sweeping of all.
432._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com's Saman Suttam (Samyamasutra) page. Reasonable but partial: it covers avarice and pride but not the Kural's third fault (unworthy delight), and it is not addressed to rulers.

433.quote_or_event: “One should not be complacent with a small debt, slight wound, spark of fire and slight passion, because what is small (today) may become bigger (later).”
433.explanation: Jain teaching treats even a slight stirring of passion (kashāya) as dangerous, comparing it to a small debt, wound or spark that grows if neglected.
433.tie_back: Those who dread disgrace, says Valluvar, treat a millet-sized fault as if it were as large as a palmyra; the Jain verse gives the same reason for refusing to belittle a small fault: what is small today grows large tomorrow.
433._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com's Saman Suttam (Samyamasutra) page. Near one-to-one on magnifying small faults, though the Kural's motive is shame before blame, while the Jain verse rests on the danger of growth.

434.quote_or_event: “Self is the one invincible foe, (together with the four) cardinal passions, (viz. anger, pride, deceit, and greed, they are five) and the (five) senses (make ten). These (foes), O great sage, I have regularly vanquished.”
434.explanation: Asked who the thousand foes attacking him are, Gautama answers that the real enemies are within: the unsubdued self, the four passions and the five senses.
434.tie_back: Valluvar insists that it is fault itself that is the enemy bringing ruin; Gautama likewise locates the true enemy in one's own faults rather than in any outside attacker.
434._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on fault as the true enemy; the Kural's added advice to guard against fault as one's chief aim (or treasure) is implied here, not stated.

435.quote_or_event: “As in a forest, full of fuel, a fire fanned by the wind cannot be extinguished, so the fire (as it were) of the senses of him who eats as he lists; it does not benefit any chaste man.”
435.explanation: The lecture on carelessness warns that once indulgence feeds the senses, their fire spreads like a wind-fanned forest blaze that can no longer be put out, so restraint must come first.
435.tie_back: Valluvar's life that fails to guard against faults before they come burns like a straw stack before a fire; the Jain image is the same, ready fuel and a fire that cannot be stopped once it catches.
435._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit in imagery and in the logic of prevention, though the Jain verse is about the senses and diet specifically, while the Kural speaks of faults in general.

436.quote_or_event: “Fight with your Self; why fight with external foes? He who conquers himself through himself, will obtain happiness.”
436.explanation: When Indra urges King Nami to subdue the princes who do not acknowledge him, Nami answers that the battle that matters is against oneself, and that only self-conquest brings happiness.
436.tie_back: Valluvar tells the ruler to remove his own faults before examining others'; Nami, also a king, likewise turns from the faults and hostility of others to the work of correcting himself.
436._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: it puts self-correction first but does not speak of then judging others' faults, which is the Kural's second step.

437.quote_or_event: “Or he heaps up treasures for the benefit of some spendthrifts, by pinching himself.” … “Then at one time, his manifold savings are a large treasure. Then at another time, his heirs divide it, or those who are without a living steal it, or the king takes it away, or it is ruined in some way or other, or it is consumed by the conflagration of the house.”
437.explanation: The Acaranga describes the man who starves himself to pile up wealth, only to have it divided by heirs, stolen, seized by the king, or burnt with his house, so that he gets no good from it.
437.tie_back: Valluvar says the miser's wealth, never put to its proper use, will perish without benefit to anyone; the Acaranga lists the very ways in which hoarded wealth slips away.
437.source: Acaranga Sutra I.2.1.4 and I.2.3.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
437._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Close fit. The Jain remedy, however, is non-possession (aparigraha) rather than the Kural's right use of wealth through giving and enjoyment.

438.quote_or_event: “If there were numberless mountains of gold and silver, as big as Kailâsa, they would not satisfy a greedy man; for his avidity is boundless like space.”
438.explanation: Refusing Indra's advice to fill his treasury, Nami answers that greed has no limit: no amount of wealth can ever satisfy a grasping heart.
438.tie_back: Valluvar sets the clinging, miserly heart apart from every other fault; Nami likewise describes avarice as boundless, unlike any fault that can be measured or satisfied.
438._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong thematic fit on greed as a fault without limit, though the verse speaks of insatiable craving rather than miserliness (refusing to give) as such.

439.quote_or_event: “'Frequently (I have been born) in a high family, frequently in a low one; I am not mean, nor noble, nor do I desire (social preferment).' Thus reflecting, who would brag about his family or about his glory, or for what should he long?”
439.explanation: The Acaranga undercuts self-admiration by reminding the aspirant that across countless rebirths each soul has been both high and low, so pride in birth or glory has no ground.
439.tie_back: Valluvar forbids admiring oneself at any time; the Acaranga gives a distinctly Jain reason for the same rule: through rebirth, every status one might boast of has already been held and lost many times.
439.source: Acaranga Sutra I.2.3.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
439._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit for the Kural's first clause (no self-admiration); its second clause, not desiring profitless deeds, is touched on only in 'for what should he long?'

440.quote_or_event: “Just as an impassioned fish which is eager to swallow the bait, has its body transfixed by a hook.” … “Just as an impassioned elephant who is inflamed by carnal desires, is turned from his way by a female elephant (and is captured and at last killed in battle).”
440.explanation: The lecture on carelessness shows how each creature is trapped through its own known craving: the fish through its appetite for bait, the elephant through desire. Whoever knows the craving can use it to catch the creature.
440.tie_back: Valluvar warns that desires known to enemies become the means of their schemes; the Jain similes show the same mechanism, though Jainism's remedy is to give up the craving, not to hide it.
440._accuracy_note: Next-best match, checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's summary of the repeated verse sets). Jainism does not endorse the Kural's strategy of enjoying desires while concealing them; it shares only the insight that a craving is a vulnerability others can exploit.
